title: Fractal Geometry for Evolutionary Algorithms
abstract: This paper explores the application of fractal geometry to enhance evolutionary algorithms, specifically focusing on the creation of complex terrain and the generation of diverse solutions. We propose a novel framework wherein landscape representation is achieved through fractal tiles, repeatedly combined and modified through evolutionary selection. The core claim is that this approach offers a new perspective on evolutionary algorithms, potentially leading to more effective solutions for complex optimization problems. The method leverages the inherent properties of fractals – self-similarity, infinite detail, and sensitivity to initial conditions – to provide a robust and adaptable tool for exploring high-dimensional search spaces. The paper details the framework's mathematical foundation and outlines a preliminary implementation demonstrating its effectiveness in generating novel landscapes.

title: Based on Nonlinear Control Theory: Quantum System Regulation
abstract: This paper investigates the application of nonlinear control theory to the precise regulation of quantum systems. Traditional control methods often struggle with the inherent complexities and sensitivities of quantum systems. This work proposes a novel approach leveraging nonlinear control techniques to directly manipulate quantum state evolution. The core claim is that by designing appropriate nonlinear control signals, it is possible to achieve precise control over quantum system dynamics. The central mechanism involves the targeted modulation of quantum motion using these nonlinear signals, ultimately enabling accurate state control. This approach overcomes the limitations of linear control methods and offers a fundamentally new way to interact with and manage quantum systems. We explore the theoretical framework, mathematical formulations, and potential applications of this approach, focusing on the design and implementation of control strategies for quantum systems. The presented methodology provides a robust and adaptable framework for quantum system regulation, promising significant advancements in quantum technologies.

title: Dynamic Probability Field Theory (DPF) Algorithm
abstract: This paper presents a novel Dynamic Probability Field Theory (DPF) algorithm designed to enhance model training efficiency and generalization ability in signal processing and machine learning. Traditional model training methods often rely on fixed parameters, limiting their adaptability to complex data and uncertainty. The proposed DPF algorithm incorporates a feedback mechanism that automatically adjusts model parameters based on training error, offering a more responsive and streamlined training process. We detail the core mechanism, highlighting its impact on model behavior and the resulting improvements in model accuracy and robustness. This research addresses a crucial limitation in machine learning, enabling the creation of more reliable and adaptable models.

title: Multi-Agent Collaboration for Robot Task Planning
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to robot task planning leveraging the principles of multi-agent collaboration. Traditional task planning methods often struggle with complex environments and inherent uncertainties, frequently relying on centralized control which can be inefficient and fragile. Our approach addresses these limitations by modeling robots as individual agents, each responsible for a specific aspect of the overall task. Through the implementation of multi-agent collaboration algorithms, we enable distributed planning and execution, leading to improved task efficiency, robustness, and adaptability. The core claim of this work is to utilize the mechanisms of multi-agent collaboration to mitigate the complexity and uncertainty inherent in robot task planning. The key mechanism involves the modeling of robots as multiple intelligent agents, each handling a portion of the task, coupled with multi-agent collaboration algorithms for distributed planning and execution. This represents a shift from centralized control to a more scalable and resilient solution.

title: Self-Organizing Neural Networks with Dynamic Topology
abstract: This paper investigates the limitations of static neural network architectures in achieving optimal performance and adaptability within complex and evolving environments. The core proposition is that a dynamic topology, capable of self-organization, offers a superior approach. We introduce a novel neural network framework designed to iteratively refine its topology based on input data and learning progress. The proposed system utilizes a self-organizing mechanism to dynamically adjust network connections and node structure, aiming to improve learning efficiency and robustness. This work highlights a significant advancement in neural network design, shifting the focus from predefined structures to adaptable, evolving systems. The key components include a modular network design, a dynamic connection weighting mechanism, and a node addition/removal strategy, all governed by a self-organizing algorithm. Experimental results, although not presented through traditional experimental sections, demonstrate the potential of this approach to outperform static networks in simulated scenarios. The research contributes to the growing field of adaptive neural networks and lays the groundwork for future exploration in dynamic learning systems.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Programming with Adaptive Rule Induction
abstract: This paper introduces a novel neuro-symbolic programming framework designed to overcome the limitations of traditional hybrid systems that heavily rely on manually defined rules. The core innovation lies in an adaptive rule induction algorithm where a neural network actively learns to generate and refine symbolic rules based on observed data. This creates a symbiotic relationship between neural and symbolic computation, enhancing adaptability and generalizability. The system employs a dynamic rule set adjustment mechanism, responding to performance metrics and uncertainty estimates. We demonstrate the potential of this approach through a theoretical framework outlining the key components and operational principles. This work addresses the critical need for more flexible and robust neuro-symbolic systems, paving the way for intelligent systems capable of learning and reasoning in complex, evolving environments. The system utilizes a recurrent neural network (RNN) to process data and a symbolic rule engine to execute and refine the learned rules. The core of the system is the adaptive rule induction algorithm, which governs the evolution of the symbolic rule set.

title: ##基于符号推理的深度学习优化 (BSSLDO)
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach, Based Symbolic Reasoning on Deep Learning Optimization (BSSLDO), which aims to enhance the generalization ability and interpretability of deep learning models by integrating symbolic reasoning techniques. BSSLDO leverages symbolic reasoning to perform structured analysis of deep learning models, providing insights into their internal workings. These insights are then utilized to guide the optimization process, resulting in improved model performance and increased transparency. The core claim of this work is that the combination of symbolic reasoning and deep learning can significantly improve the latter's capabilities. We present a framework for BSSLDO and discuss its potential applications and future research directions. The proposed method addresses a critical limitation of current deep learning approaches – the 'black box' nature – by introducing a structured and interpretable layer of reasoning. Our approach offers a pathway to developing more robust and reliable deep learning systems. ---

title: Title: Adaptive Phase-Coherence Synchronization for Quantum Algorithms
abstract: Quantum algorithms rely heavily on precise phase-coherence, a delicate phenomenon crucial for computation. Current synchronization protocols often employ fixed parameters, limiting the algorithm's performance. This paper investigates and presents an adaptive phase-coherence synchronization protocol, designed to dynamically adjust synchronization parameters based on the evolving phase-coherence dynamics of quantum systems. We propose a novel approach that leverages a feedback mechanism to optimize synchronization fidelity, addressing limitations of existing methods and opening avenues for enhanced quantum algorithm execution. The core mechanism involves a self-regulating algorithm that continually monitors the quantum state and adjusts synchronization parameters to maintain optimal phase-coherence. This adaptability will significantly improve the fidelity of quantum algorithms, offering a more robust and efficient solution.

title: Optimizing Referee Assignments with Fuzzy Evaluation and Particle Swarm Intelligence
abstract: Referee assignment is a recurring challenge in a wide range of settings—from assigning officials to sports matches to allocating reviewers for academic conferences. These scenarios often involve complex constraints, such as assigning multiple referees to a single activity or allowing referees to evaluate multiple tasks. In this study, we address a generalized version of the referee assignment problem, focusing on the case where each activity is matched with exactly one referee. To evaluate the suitability of assignments, we leverage rating scores across multiple dimensions for both referees and activities. These scores are incorporated into fuzzy membership functions that quantify assignment quality. We propose a Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) algorithm that uses these fuzzy-based evaluations to guide the search for optimal assignments. Synthetic datasets with varying levels of data dispersion—generated from uniform distributions with equal means but different variances—are used to test the algorithm. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed PSO approach is not only computationally efficient but also robust across different variance scenarios. This method offers a flexible and adaptable solution for a broad class of referee-assignment problems.

title: Multi-USVs Collaborative Water Pollution Traceability and Source Localization Using an Improved Wolf Pack Algorithm
abstract: With the increasing frequency of water pollution incidents due to urbanization and industrialization, this paper proposes an Improved Wolf Pack Algorithm (IWPA) for coordinating multiple Unmanned Surface Vessels (USVs) to achieve rapid river pollution traceability. The IWPA incorporates a dynamic step adjustment mechanism and a dynamic population adjustment strategy to overcome the limitations of the fixed step factor and random repositioning in the standard Wolf Pack Algorithm (WPA). These enhancements prevent the algorithm from converging on local optima and improve the overall traceability efficiency of the multi-USV formation. Simulation results demonstrate the superior performance of IWPA. Under conditions of a 1500 g/s source emission rate, a 3 m/s longitudinal flow velocity, and using only 5 USVs, IWPA achieves a success rate of 97.3% and an average localization error of 0.41 m. These results represent improvements of 15.9% in success rate and 71.3% in error reduction compared to the standard WPA. Laboratory-based water pollution traceability tests further confirm the method’s effectiveness, with a success rate of 80%, validating its practical localization capability.

title: Quantum Machine Learning Frameworks for Data Analysis
abstract: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) frameworks present a new paradigm for data analysis that uses the parallelism and entanglement of quantum computing to facilitate efficient learning. In this paper we introduce a new robust, scalable and hybrid QML framework to address shortcomings of existing models, such as sensitivity to noise, scalability, and interpretability. By combining quantum kernel methods, variational circuits, and hybrid training routines, the framework offers practical data applications in finance, healthcare and cybersecurity. Its scalability and versatility are supported by benchmarks over simulators and true quantum hardware. This work paves the way for future-proof modular quantum-enhanced data analytics systems.

title: Legal text classification in Korean sexual offense cases: from traditional machine learning to large language models with XAI insights
abstract: The advancement of natural language processing (NLP) has expanded AI-based text classification in the legal domain. However, accurately classifying legal documents remains challenging due to the complexity of legal texts and subtle differences between legal categories. This study evaluates legal text classification models ranging from traditional machine learning techniques to large language models (LLMs) using ten categories of Korean sexual offense precedents. The results show that fine-tuning small-scale models such as KLUE-BERT on legal data outperforms general-purpose models such as GPT-3.5 and GPT-4.0, as well as traditional machine learning models. KLUE-BERT achieved the highest accuracy of 99.3%, indicating that domain adaptation and fine-tuning can be more important than model size for legal document classification. We further employ explainable AI (XAI) techniques to analyze model predictions and misclassification cases. XAI analysis identifies linguistic features influencing model decisions and limitations in capturing subtle textual cues. Using KICS data, which closely resembles real-world legal case records, we further evaluate the model's generalization capabilities and find that it struggles to interpret implicit contextual cues. These findings highlight the importance of both performance and interpretability in legal AI and demonstrate how XAI can improve transparency in legal text classification. AI-assisted tools can support legal professionals in tasks including document classification, legal information retrieval, and case assessment.

title: Threshold Choice, Not Sample Size, Bounds Trustless Verification of Nondeterministic Compound AI Workflows
abstract: Compound AI pipelines chain LLM calls, retrievers, and tools and are nondeterministic: sampling, model updates, and volatile tool responses make one input yield different outputs across runs. Such pipelines increasingly run across edge, cloud, and orbital nodes owned by no single party, whose optimizations discard intermediate results before inspection. Verifying reproduction there means tolerating nondeterministic outputs, a node that may not report honestly, and intermittent access to any shared record; existing work addresses at most two at once. We give a protocol covering all three: it commits digests of each stage's inputs, outputs, and context under a policy digest pinning the metric and threshold, anchors them without trusting the executing node, defers under partition, and decides a challenge on the median of $k$ re-executions, with no quorum. Where that procedure breaks is the main result. On a synthetic HotpotQA pipeline a calibrated fixed threshold accepts 44 of 45 honest reproductions and rejects 104 of 105 divergent pairs, yet lets same-input fabrication through in 27 of 29 trials at k=5, more samples being no help since sampling sharpens an estimate without moving it. Holding that metric and this pipeline's re-execution spread fixed, the binding constraint is the threshold rather than the sample size: one derived per execution detects 19 of 29 where the best constant matched to the same zero honest rejections reaches 9, rejects no honest commitment at k=5 though 3 of 15 at k=3, and catches 11 of 15 of an attacker built against it, which has to aim at a target drawn only after its commitment exists. That rule is measured rather than deployed.

title: Where Should Language Sit in a Multimodal Model? Lessons from What Language Does to Human Perception and Cognition
abstract: Language models compute over tokens: language is their input, their output, and increasingly their internal representation. Whether language should keep all of these positions depends on what language does to the system that uses it. The one system with a century of data on that question is the human. We review what language does to human perception, the brain, and thought, and read the same evidence against multimodal models and language models. Throughout, we treat language as a compressor that runs on a shared codebook: a word is an index, the content is in the receiver, and a community maintains the codebook. In humans the compression is measurable, learning the codebook reorganizes the senses, and thought survives the loss of language. We then measure the rule that models apply when two cues disagree, with cue-conflict experiments on six vision-language models and two robot policies. Surviving cues are weighted in the order their reliabilities prescribe, at 11 to 82\% of the ideal observer's slope, and many answers copy the text. One policy family drops a cue that adds no information beyond the others rather than down-weighting it, another keeps it at a weight that fails when the cues conflict, and a visual cue that identifies the task in every training frame is never learned, because the language pathway already fits the data. Language models are the best current models of the human language network, and they have entered the human speech community, shifting word frequencies while alignment narrows their conceptual diversity. We close with seven implications for token-based systems. Language belongs at a model's boundary and in the shared codebook, as in the brain, not as its internal representation; the price of leaving the codebook inside is auditability.

title: Emo-DVS: A Multimodal Benchmark for Privacy-Aware Emotion Recognition with Event Cameras
abstract: Emotion analysis is a fundamental task in computer vision, but its practical deployment remains constrained by the privacy risks inherent to conventional RGB cameras. Bio-inspired event cameras present a promising hardware-level solution because they capture asynchronous brightness changes, thereby reducing exposure of facial identity details while leveraging high dynamic range for robust perception under challenging illumination conditions. Despite these advantages, existing event-based methods struggle in complex real-world settings due to limited dataset scales, simple acquisition conditions, and reliance on single-modality visual cues. To address these, we establish a challenging tri-modal benchmark with event, audio, and text modalities and propose the Information-Guided Gated Fusion (IGF) framework, which first pre-trains an event encoder on the FAU subset of Emo-DVS to capture fine-grained facial dynamics, then employs adaptive modality gating to suppress modality-specific noise, and finally leverages mutual information maximization to align robust cross-modal representations. To alleviate data scarcity, we introduce Emo-DVS, the first large-scale event-based emotion analysis dataset, which couples dynamic illumination with the Facial Action Unit (FAU) subset and emotion subset. Extensive experiments demonstrate that IGF achieves state-of-the-art performance.

title: SPARROW: Scalable Taxonomy Induction via Structure-Preserving Partitioning and Constraint-Guided Merging
abstract: Taxonomy induction aims to organize concept sets into coherent hierarchical structures. Recent LLM-based methods can induce taxonomies directly from flat term lists, avoiding the need for corpora, but degrade sharply as concept sets scale up. We argue that this degradation stems not only from context length limitations, but also from structural failures in hierarchical reasoning. To address this, we adopt a divide-and-merge paradigm that partitions concepts into smaller subsets, induces local taxonomies, and merges them into a global hierarchy. However, we identify two structural failure modes inherent to this paradigm: Structural Fragmentation, where partitioning weakens local hierarchical signals, and Parent Displacement, where locally plausible relations are misplaced in the global hierarchy. To address both, we propose SPARROW, a scalable taxonomy induction framework that combines structure-preserving spectral partitioning to retain hierarchical connectivity within each block, and constraint-guided incremental fusion that treats block-level relations as structural constraints rather than ground truth for global placement. Experiments on large-scale benchmarks show that SPARROW consistently achieves the strongest global structural quality across backbones. The code is available at https://github.com/rebeccazyr/SPARROW.

title: Translation of Black-Box Clinical Prediction Models into Standalone Transparent Nomograms: Temporal External Validation in Heart Transplantation
abstract: We convert black-box clinical prediction models for tabular data into standalone nomograms that can be audited term by term. PRiSM (Partial Responses in Structured Models) takes the shape of each effect and interaction from the source model, not merely which variables mattered, and lets the outcome select and weight them. We tested this in 50,356 heart transplant recipients, with validation in a later era than training. Nomograms from all 5 source models - a public clinical risk score, logistic regression, neural networks, random forests and extreme gradient boosting - met a prespecified noninferiority criterion for discrimination before any further simplification, and generally preserved calibration and clinical net benefit. Those from the 3 machine-learning models showed no detectable difference in discrimination from de novo generalized additive and explainable boosting models, exceeded neural additive models, and carried fewer terms than the explainable boosting model. PRiSM is released as an open-source Python package.

evidence.title: PRiSM (Partial Responses in Structured Models): a Python framework for converting probabilistic binary classifiers into auditable nomograms
evidence.abstract: PRiSM (Partial Responses in Structured Models) is a model-agnostic framework that converts a trained probabilistic binary classifier for tabular data into a standalone nomogram that can be audited term by term. PRiSM takes the shape of each nonlinear effect and interaction from the source model, not merely which variables mattered, and lets the observed outcome select and weight them. The result is an additive model that replaces the original classifier as the deployed predictor. Because the nomogram is additive on the log-odds scale, each variable's contribution can be read off and summed by hand. PRiSM is a collaboration between the Artificial Intelligence and Bioinformatics in Cardiothoracic Sciences Research Unit at Lund University, Sweden, and the Artificial Intelligence and Digital Technologies Research Institute at Liverpool John Moores University, UK. The framework is authored by: Henry Pigot (1), Paulo J. G. Lisboa (2), Sandra Ortega-Martorell (2), Ivan Olier (2), Joseph Mahon (2), Johan Nilsson (1,3) (1) Department of Translational Medicine, Artificial Intelligence and Bioinformatics in Cardiothoracic Sciences Research Unit, Lund University, Lund, Sweden (2) Artificial Intelligence and Digital Technologies Research Institute, Liverpool John Moores University, Liverpool, UK (3) Department of Thoracic and Vascular Surgery, Skåne University Hospital, Lund, Sweden This record archives the v0.1.0 source release. title: RouteRelay: Event-Triggered Cross-Layer Route Reuse for Efficient Dynamic Sparse Attention
abstract: Dynamic sparse attention reduces long-context prefill cost by routing each query chunk to a small set of key chunks at every Transformer layer. The sparse attention kernel avoids most token interactions, but the router still rebuilds a chunk--chunk score matrix layer after layer, even when the selected routes change little. We introduce RouteRelay, a router-agnostic method that reuses only route metadata across depth while continuing to compute attention with the current layer's queries, keys, and values. Anchor layers perform full routing. Intermediate layers rescore the previous top-$k$ route and a compact sentinel set of near-miss and randomly probed chunks. A query row is rerouted only when a sentinel challenges its weakest selected chunk. We give a top-$k$ stability condition, a probabilistic bound on missed challengers, and a row-selective GPU execution design. In a reproducible empirical evaluation, RouteRelay retains at least 99.99% route recall while rerouting 25.0%, 55.4%, and 78.2% of rows under low, moderate, and high cross-layer drift, respectively. Across routing scales, RouteRelay retains 100.0% recall while evaluating 38.4--51.6% of full-routing score pairs as the key-chunk count grows from 128 to 1024. Its unfused CPU execution remains slower than dense matrix multiplication, exposing row compaction and ledger updates as the main kernel-engineering targets.

title: The Internal Anatomy of Strategic Choice in Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models act as strategic agents and models of human choice, yet choosing like a strategic agent does not mean computing like one. We recorded activations from four open-weight models --- dense and mixture-of-experts, including a matched base--instruct pair --- in one-shot play of 144 strict ordinal $2\times2$ games. We followed a prespecified incentive from prompt, through activations, to choice. Dense models mirrored the unadjusted human decline with game complexity. Incentive and choice were detectable in every model, but models differed in whether incentive reached the choice, aligned with it and, where tested, whether strengthening it shifted preference. The base and instruction-tuned Qwen2.5 models chose almost identically at baseline yet differed in whether incentive reached choice. Fixed decision cues were distinguishable internally but changed choices selectively. Similar behaviour can rest on different computation; post-training can reshape the path from represented incentive to decision while leaving behaviour and decodable information largely intact.

evidence.abstract: Data deposit for The Internal Anatomy of Strategic Choice in Large Language Models (arXiv:2609.07478). Five components: substrate (residual-stream captures for the three dense models and harmony-channel captures for GPT-OSS, all 144 Robinson–Goforth/Bruns canonical 2×2 games), gptoss_recap (GPT-OSS uniform-transition-site recapture), layerc (token-attribution scores), layerc_bridge_residuals, and steering (fitted directions, small-dose and permutation steering outputs; empirical and q=0.5 arms). Analysis code and per-figure reproduction commands: github.com/vferraz/strategic-choice-anatomy. scripts/download_data.py in that repository downloads and verifies these components against its committed manifest.
